message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel numeric work – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific, machine‑learning, and other compute‑heavy tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful with deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, large caches, and complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups; each core does less work individually but many can run the same instruction simultaneously. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex, variable‑length instructions, rich set of operations, support for branching, exceptions, etc. | Simpler, fixed‑width instructions optimized for arithmetic on vectors/matrices; limited branching. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory interface, strong cache coherence across cores. | Smaller per‑core caches, often rely on shared memory pools; coherence is usually handled at a higher level or not needed for typical workloads. |
| **Parallelism** | Mostly *task* parallelism – different threads doing different things. | Mostly *data* parallelism – many threads doing the same thing on different data elements. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control‑intensive tasks, I/O, database queries, web servers, operating system kernels. | Matrix/vector math, image/video processing, physics simulations, deep learning inference/training, rendering pipelines. |
| **Power & Cost** | More power‑hungry per core, but fewer cores overall. | Many cores share power budget; cost per core is lower, but total cost scales with number of cores. |

In short, CPUs excel at serial, branching, and diverse tasks, while GPUs shine when you have a huge amount of similar calculations that can be performed in parallel. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU handles general control flow, and the GPU accelerates heavy numeric kernels.
